title: Halcyon Systems POC scoping - latency SLOs
summary: POC scoping focused on defining latency and throughput SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), workload sizing, benchmarks to run, and an initial timeline. Customer wants p95/p99 targets, measurement plan, and acceptance criteria for a 4-week pilot. Security and deployment constraints (VPC + KMS) discussed.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-12-09 15:30 PT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Evan Blake (Redwood AE), Samira Chen (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (Halcyon Head of ML), Maya Ortiz (Halcyon Platform), Liam Brooks (Halcyon Product)

[00:00] Evan: Hey everyone thanks for taking time, can you hear me ok?
[00:03] Raj: Yep good, thanks Evan, excited to get into the POC scoping.
[00:10] Samira: Great, we sent a short agenda: define success criteria, traffic patterns, target SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), and the measurement plan. Does that match what you're looking for?
[00:20] Maya: Yeah that's perfect. Our main ask is that the model responses be snappy for interactive features. We also need to validate batch throughput for nightly jobs.
[00:30] Liam: Timeline wise, product wants a 4-week pilot to make a go/no-go decision by end of Jan.
[00:36] Evan: Cool, makes sense. Raj, quick context — what's your current stack and who'll be the exec sign-off?
[00:43] Raj: We're running inference on-prem right now, mix of Nvidia A100s and some T4s for smaller workloads. Exec sign-off will be me + CTO for production. We're sensitive about data residency, everything must sit in our VPC or on-prem, keys managed in our KMS.
[00:58] Samira: Totally understood, Redwood Private supports VPC deployments and customer-managed KMS/HSM. We'll include the security docs.
[01:05] Raj: Thanks. On SLAs we care about perceived latency for users — so TTFT and also p95 for full response for short prompts. For our analytics batch jobs we care about TPOT and overall throughput.
[01:18] Evan: Can we define concrete numbers? For interactive chat, what's acceptable p95 and p99?
[01:23] Maya: Ideally p95 under 300ms TTFT and p99 under 800ms for short responses (under 200 tokens). But if p95 for full response, maybe 800ms is ok? We're flexible if you explain tradeoffs.
[01:36] Raj: For TPOT on batch scoring we want 5ms per token p95 during steady state, and throughput of 20k tokens/sec for the nightly window.
[01:45] Samira: Good — couple clarifications: when you say TTFT 300ms, do you mean time-to-first-token from request ingress to first byte out including network to our hosted endpoint or from within your VPC?
[01:55] Raj: From user to response, so includes network across our infra. For the POC we can measure within the VPC and add measured egress latency.
[02:04] Evan: Ok that implies we need a measurement plan with synthetic and real traffic capture. We'll need a baseline run to capture your network latency then run identical workload against Redwood Private.
[02:13] Liam: For workload sizing — our interactive traffic is about 200 QPS at peak, average payload ~120 tokens in and 180 tokens out. Nightly batch is roughly 2B tokens over an hour window.
[02:25] Samira: Nice, those numbers are helpful. For the POC we typically do: 1) a functional smoke test, 2) latency bench (TTFT/TPOT) with synthetic traffic that mimics your payload distribution, 3) throughput ramp to validate autoscaling and Dedicated capacity, 4) end-to-end quality checks.
[02:40] Raj: Sounds good. How do you measure TPOT? Is that per-token time in the model or includes batching overhead?
[02:46] Samira: Our TPOT measurement is server-side per-token emission time measured at the model output stage; it includes batching overhead and kernel execution. For end-user TPOT you'd add network and prefix cache hit penalty. We report p50/p95/p99 and can break out kernel vs queue time.
[02:59] Evan: We'll share an artifacts checklist: benchmark scripts, latency harness, and a small dataset of representative prompts. We'll also provide a short doc describing how we compute TTFT and TPOT (note: sometimes speech-to-text mislabels TTFT as T-T-F-T in our older docs).
[03:12] Maya: Cool. Any competitors you recommend comparing against? We ran a quick comparison to OpenAI's hosted API but weren't happy with cost or control.
[03:20] Raj: Also looking at Anthropic and Vertex.
[03:23] Evan: We'll include a competitor note but the POC will focus on meeting your SLOs on our infra.
[03:28] Samira: On SLOs — recommend defining acceptance criteria like: 1) TTFT p95 <= 300ms and p99 <= 800ms for interactive (under 200 tokens) measured from e2e within VPC; 2) TPOT server-side p95 <= 6ms and p99 <= 12ms for steady state; 3) Throughput >= 20k tokens/sec sustained for 5 minutes during the batch window and no errors above 0.1%.
[03:50] Liam: That seems reasonable. The TPOT p99 of 12ms is ok as long as user-facing metrics are within our targets.
[03:57] Raj: We also want to understand tail behavior under autoscale events — how does Redwood degrade? Are there fallbacks?
[04:05] Samira: We have automated fallbacks to smaller model variants and capacity tiers. For Private deployments we can configure routing policies and warm pools. We'll simulate autoscale spikes during the ramp tests.
[04:16] Evan: For measurement, proposal: 1) synthetic driver inside your VPC to generate realistic QPS and token distribution; 2) ingest server-side metrics (Redwood agent) for kernel/queue times; 3) client-side probes to measure e2e TTFT and full response. We'll correlate logs and provide dashboards.
[04:31] Maya: Who sets up the driver? Our infra or Redwood?
[04:34] Samira: We can provide the harness and help deploy it as a docker container in your VPC; Raj's team can run it with our instructions.
[04:42] Raj: Ok that works. For security review, send SOC2 and ISO certs and details on how KMS integration works. Also need audit log format.
[04:51] Evan: We'll attach the security pack and a sample audit log schema.
[04:55] Liam: For observability, we want token-level cost and latency breakdowns — is that in the console?
[05:00] Samira: Yes, Redwood Console will show per-route and per-request breakdowns. We'll provide dashboard links in the POC.
[05:07] Raj: Alright timeline — can we kick off next Monday? We need a 1-week setup then 3 weeks of testing to hit Jan deadline.
[05:14] Evan: That's feasible. Proposed timeline: Week 0 (setup): deploy agent + harness, data prep. Week 1: baseline runs and smallscale latency tests. Week 2: throughput ramp and autoscale tests. Week 3: stability run + acceptance and handoff.
[05:27] Maya: Works for us. Any blockers?
[05:30] Samira: Need access to a staging VPC and someone from your infra to approve deployment of the harness and accept our agent.
[05:37] Raj: I'll assign an infra owner.
[05:39] Evan: Great. A few clarifying Qs on acceptance criteria: do you want us to include both TTFT and full-response p95/p99 as separate gates?
[05:47] Liam: Yes, two gates. TTFT matters for first-impression; full-response for completion-sensitive flows.
[05:52] Samira: Noted. We'll produce an acceptance doc with exact measurement windows, test scripts, and thresholds.
[05:58] Raj: Also include how you handle KV cache warm vs cold runs — that changes TTFT significantly.
[06:04] Samira: Good point. We'll do cold-start and warm-cache scenarios. We'll also measure prefix caching hit rates. Sometimes silence in transcriptions calls it K-V cash, haha.
[06:15] Evan: Ok let's recap next steps...

[06:18] Raj: Great recap please.

[06:20] Evan: We'll share: security pack, benchmark harness repo, measurement plan doc, and a proposed SLA/acceptance doc. Samira will own the benchmark setup. Action items below.

[06:30] Maya: Thanks everyone.
[06:32] Liam: Thanks Evan, Samira.
[06:34] Evan: Bye all.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-attribution and faint words; some acronyms may be mis-transcribed (e.g., TTFT as T-T-F-T, TPOT as T-P-O-T), natural pauses and crosstalk present.
